claims.text: The baseline alloy is equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni.
The quinary alloy and the selected quaternary and ternary subsets can all be prepared as single-phase FCC materials by thermomechanical processing.
Systematically removing one or more constituents while retaining an equivalent processing history provides the controlled compositional intervention.
Removing specific elements such as Mn modifies local lattice distortions.
Removing specific elements such as Mn modifies solute-dislocation interactions.
Changes in local lattice distortion and solute-dislocation interactions alter slip-system activation.
Altered slip-system activation changes deformation and failure behavior relative to the quinary baseline.
Removing elements such as Mn alters magnetic interactions.
Removing elements such as Mn alters the stacking-fault-energy landscape.
Removing elements such as Mn reduces local lattice distortion.

Changes in magnetic interactions, stacking-fault energy, lattice distortion, and solute-dislocation interactions modify the balance among dislocation slip, twinning, and incipient phase transformation.
Quaternary and ternary subsets will show less local lattice distortion than the quinary alloy under identical deformation conditions.
Quaternary and ternary subsets will exhibit altered slip-system activation relative to the quinary alloy.
Quaternary and ternary subsets may exhibit lower twinning activity than the quinary alloy.
Quaternary and ternary subsets may fail prematurely relative to the quinary alloy.
The comparison is restricted to room-temperature deformation at a common defined strain rate and equivalent thermomechanical processing.
In situ diffraction and electron microscopy can compare lattice strain, dislocation-density evolution, active slip systems, twinning fraction, and phase-transformation indicators across the alloys.
A lack of significant differences in the proposed mediators and slip activity under identical conditions would falsify the claim that those mediators explain the mechanical-property differences.
